lesson.title: Doubling the Republic: Jefferson's Fifteen Million Dollar Gamble
lesson.summary: Jefferson's 1803 purchase of the Louisiana Territory from France roughly doubled the size of the United States, forcing the strict constructionist president to set aside his own constitutional principles for the sake of national opportunity.
lesson.body:
When Thomas Jefferson became president in 1801, one of his most pressing concerns was control of the port of New Orleans, the vital outlet through which farmers in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys shipped their goods to market. Spain had controlled Louisiana for decades, but in a secret 1800 treaty it transferred the territory back to France, raising alarm in Washington that Napoleon Bonaparte might close the port or use Louisiana as a base to rebuild a French empire in North America, reviving the kind of European rivalry over the continent that had shaped Jefferson's earlier years as Secretary of State negotiating with France, Spain, and Britain.

Jefferson sent Robert Livingston, and later James Monroe, to Paris in 1803 with instructions to negotiate the purchase of New Orleans and West Florida for as much as ten million dollars. Napoleon, however, had just suffered a catastrophic setback, a French army sent to crush the revolution led by Toussaint Louverture and reclaim the valuable colony of Saint Domingue, modern Haiti, had been decimated by yellow fever and fierce resistance, ruining Napoleon's hopes of using Louisiana to supply a Caribbean empire. Facing renewed war with Britain and needing cash, Napoleon startled the American negotiators by offering to sell the entire Louisiana Territory, not just New Orleans.

Livingston and Monroe, without authority for a deal this large, agreed anyway, and the two sides settled on a price of roughly fifteen million dollars for around eight hundred thousand square miles of land stretching from the Mississippi River toward the Rocky Mountains, an area that would eventually form all or part of more than a dozen future states. The purchase roughly doubled the size of the United States overnight and eliminated a major European power's foothold on the continent's interior.

The deal put Jefferson in an uncomfortable position. As a lifelong strict constructionist who had once argued that the federal government possessed no power beyond what the Constitution explicitly listed, most notably during the national bank debate, Jefferson worried that nothing in the Constitution authorized the president to acquire new territory by treaty. He briefly considered proposing a constitutional amendment to make the purchase legitimate, but concerned that Napoleon might withdraw the offer during the delay, Jefferson ultimately set his constitutional scruples aside and submitted the treaty to the Senate, which ratified it in October 1803.

The Louisiana Purchase transformed the young nation's future, opening vast lands for settlement and agriculture that fit neatly with Jefferson's vision of an expanding republic of independent farmers, central to what became known as Jeffersonian Democracy. It also raised urgent questions about what lay within this newly acquired territory, questions Jefferson moved quickly to answer by organizing an expedition, led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, to map the land, chart a route to the Pacific, and establish relations with the many Native nations who already lived across the territory the United States had just claimed on paper.
